Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Liam, a 28-year-old financial analyst living in a quiet suburb of Chicago, had been married for four years when his life was subsumed by a single, terrifying week. His two-year-old daughter, Maya, had developed a sudden, high fever that escalated into febrile seizures. He remembered the ambulance ride with a clarity that felt like a curse: the precise grey of the clouds outside the window, the specific, rhythmic hum of the siren, the way the rain began to fall just as they reached the hospital. The memory was not a story he could tell; it was a series of vivid, intrusive pictures that would flash behind his eyes without warning—the pale blue of the hospital sheets, the frantic beeping of the monitors, the exact angle of the doctor’s head as he delivered the prognosis. He could never get to the end of that memory. Every time he tried to recall the moment the doctors said she would be fine, his mind would slam shut, blocking the sequence before it was complete, leaving him stranded in the most frightening part of the image reel.

In the months that followed Maya’s full recovery, Liam did not return to the man he had been. He had come to believe that the person sitting in his office, running spreadsheets and analyzing market trends, was a stranger. The person he had become was unrecognisable to him. He felt as though his old self—the easy-going husband, the confident analyst—had been erased, replaced by a creature of pure vigilance. He was certain that he had failed. The thought was a splinter that had worked its way deep under his skin: *I should have protected her. I should have known. I failed.* This conviction colored everything. He no longer trusted his own judgment, his own calm, his own right to feel safe.

His job as a financial analyst, once a source of pride and structure, had become a landscape of hidden threats. The open-plan office, with its rows of desks and lack of clear sightlines to the exits, made his skin crawl. Before he could sit down and open his laptop, he had to scan the room, noting every door, every stairwell, every possible route to the outside. He could not help it; the compulsion was automatic, a ritual he performed without conscious thought. When a coworker would suddenly appear at his desk, or when the fire alarm was tested, his body would lurch into a full-blown emergency response—heart hammering, breath shallow, a cold certainty that something terrible was about to happen. He knew it was a false alarm, but knowing did nothing to stop the reaction. He would sit there, trembling, trying to mask the panic, while everyone else laughed at the surprise drill.

At home, the vigilance was worse. He had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, listening for any change in Maya’s breathing, any cough, any silence that felt too long. He would lie rigid in the dark, his mind cycling through escape routes from the bedroom, from the house, from the neighborhood. The weather became a trigger. Every time the sky turned the same shade of grey as it had on that day, he would feel a wave of nausea, certain that a new disaster was about to unfold. He found himself avoiding the news entirely, flinching at headlines about childhood illnesses, and he began to pull away from friends who had children, because being around them only reminded him of what could happen. The consequence was a quiet, creeping isolation. His wife, Sarah, began to complain that he was never fully present, that he was always scanning, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. He had stopped agreeing to playdates, stopped taking Maya to the park on overcast days, stopped living the life they had built.

What finally brought Liam to seek help was a single, mundane moment. He was driving home from work, and the sky was clear, and the radio was playing a song he used to love. For a split second, he felt nothing. No fear, no scanning. Then, the terror hit him harder than ever—not because something bad was happening, but because he had dared to feel okay. He was terrified that letting his guard down would invite the catastrophe back. He came to the clinic because he wanted to understand why he could no longer recognize the man in the mirror, and because he was desperate to stop feeling like a failure every time his daughter smiled at him.
